dx: Adhesive small bowel obstruction after appendectomy
case: A 38-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of crampy periumbilical pain, repeated bilious vomiting, and abdominal distension. He has passed no stool or flatus for 24 hours. He underwent open appendectomy for perforated appendicitis 3 years ago. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg. The abdomen is distended, with a healed right lower quadrant scar and high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds. Serum studies show Na+ 136 mEq/L (135 to 145), K+ 3.1 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), Cl- 88 mEq/L (98 to 106), and HCO3- 34 mEq/L (22 to 28). CT scan shows dilated small bowel proximal to a transition point in the right lower quadrant, with collapsed bowel distally and no hernia or mass. The diagnosis is small bowel obstruction from postoperative adhesions.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes most likely produced the fibrous band that is obstructing this patient's bowel?
options: Implantation of ectopic endometrial tissue on the peritoneum at surgery
Hypertrophic scarring of the skin incision tethering the underlying ileum
Organization of persistent serosal fibrin by fibroblasts into collagen
Granulomatous reaction to retained suture material forming a mass
approach: Note the setting: earlier surgery for perforated appendicitis, so the peritoneum was both cut and inflamed.
Injured mesothelium leaks a fibrin-rich exudate that glues nearby serosal surfaces together.
Fibrin that is not cleared becomes scaffolding for fibroblasts and new vessels, which lay down a collagen band that can kink or trap a loop of bowel.
questions.why: Surgery and peritonitis injure the mesothelium and cause a fibrinous exudate between serosal surfaces. Normally, mesothelial cells release tissue plasminogen activator, and plasmin dissolves this fibrin within days. Injury and inflammation reduce this fibrinolysis, so the fibrin persists and is organized by fibroblasts into collagen bands. These adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults who have had abdominal surgery.
whyNot: Endometriosis can cause pelvic adhesions, but it comes from retrograde menstruation or metaplasia in women. It does not arise from a surgical procedure in a man.
Skin scars stay in the dermis. They do not reach through the abdominal wall muscles to bind the bowel.
Correct.
A suture granuloma forms a small nodule of macrophages around foreign material. It does not form the long fibrous bands that obstruct bowel.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient best distinguishes his condition from adynamic ileus?
options: High-pitched bowel sounds and a CT transition point
Abdominal distension with repeated bilious vomiting
Absence of stool and flatus for the past 24 hours
Serum potassium concentration below the reference range
approach: Both mechanical obstruction and adynamic ileus cause distension, vomiting, and no passage of stool or gas, so those findings cannot separate them.
In mechanical obstruction, the bowel above the block contracts hard, which makes high-pitched, tinkling sounds.
Imaging shows dilated loops only up to one point, with collapsed bowel beyond it. In ileus, the bowel is quiet and gas is spread diffusely through small bowel and colon.
questions.why: Mechanical obstruction has a physical block. The bowel proximal to it works against the block, so bowel sounds are high pitched and rushing, and CT shows a transition point with dilated loops above and collapsed bowel below. Adynamic ileus is a failure of motility with no physical block. Bowel sounds are reduced or absent, and gas fills small bowel and colon diffusely, with no transition point.
whyNot: Correct.
Distension and vomiting occur in both conditions because contents build up in either case. They do not tell you whether a physical block is present.
Obstipation occurs in both conditions. It tells you contents are not moving forward, without telling you why.
Low potassium is a known cause of adynamic ileus, so it would point away from mechanical obstruction. Here it is a result of vomiting.

topics: Bowel sounds and imaging in obstruction

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient's kidneys have not corrected his elevated serum bicarbonate concentration?
options: Loss of pancreatic bicarbonate in the vomited intestinal fluid
Hypoaldosteronism that limits distal hydrogen ion secretion
Release of bicarbonate from bone as it buffers lost gastric acid
Chloride and volume depletion that preserve bicarbonate
approach: Read the labs: high HCO3-, low Cl-, and low K+ after days of vomiting point to a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
Vomiting removes HCl, which generates the alkalosis. Something must also stop the kidney from excreting the extra bicarbonate.
Volume loss activates renin and aldosterone, and low chloride limits bicarbonate secretion in the collecting duct, so the kidney keeps reabsorbing bicarbonate.
questions.why: Vomiting is triggered when the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema and visceral afferents from the distended gut activate the medullary vomiting center. Each liter of vomited gastric juice removes H+ and Cl-, which raises plasma bicarbonate. Volume depletion then activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which increases Na+ reabsorption with H+ and K+ secretion. Low chloride also limits the collecting duct exchanger that secretes bicarbonate in return for chloride. The kidney therefore holds on to bicarbonate until volume and chloride are replaced.
whyNot: Losing bicarbonate-rich intestinal or pancreatic fluid lowers serum bicarbonate and causes metabolic acidosis. His bicarbonate is high.
Low aldosterone reduces H+ and K+ secretion and causes a hyperkalemic acidosis. Volume loss raises aldosterone in this patient.
Bone buffers acid in chronic metabolic acidosis, releasing carbonate and calcium. Losing acid does not draw bicarbonate out of bone.
Correct.

topics: Vomiting center and chemoreceptor trigger zone

questions.stem: At laparoscopy, the obstructing band attaches a loop of ileum to the parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall. Which of the following layers forms the outer surface of the ileal wall at the site of attachment?
options: Adventitia of dense connective tissue blending into nearby tissues
Serosa of mesothelium over a thin layer of loose connective tissue
Muscularis externa with inner circular and outer longitudinal layers
Submucosa of dense irregular tissue containing the Meissner plexus
approach: Decide whether the ileum is intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal. It hangs on a mesentery, so it is intraperitoneal.
Intraperitoneal gut is covered by visceral peritoneum, which forms the serosa.
Adhesions join serosal (mesothelial) surfaces, so the band attaches to the serosa.
questions.why: The gut wall has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and an outer serosa or adventitia. Intraperitoneal segments such as the jejunum and ileum are covered by serosa, which is a mesothelium on a thin layer of loose connective tissue. Adhesions form between injured mesothelial surfaces, which is why they link loops of bowel to one another and to the parietal peritoneum.
whyNot: Adventitia covers gut that has no peritoneal covering, such as most of the esophagus and the retroperitoneal parts of the colon and duodenum. The ileum is intraperitoneal.
Correct.
The muscularis externa lies deep to the serosa. It holds the myenteric plexus between its two layers but is not the outer surface.
The submucosa lies between the mucosa and the muscularis externa. It is deep inside the wall and is not exposed to the peritoneal cavity.

case: A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a painful right groin swelling for 10 hours and three episodes of vomiting. For 2 years, he has had a right groin bulge that appeared with straining and disappeared when he lay down. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg. Physical examination shows a tense, tender, erythematous right inguinoscrotal mass that cannot be reduced. The abdomen is distended. Leukocyte count is 15,800/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000), and serum lactate concentration is 3.6 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2). At emergency surgery, the hernia sac contains a dark, edematous loop of ileum. The diagnosis is a strangulated indirect inguinal hernia.

questions.stem: Which of the following sequences of events most likely produced the dark, edematous loop of ileum?
options: Arterial occlusion at the neck of the sac, then venous thrombosis
Venous outflow blocked at the neck, then arterial inflow lost
Mucosal invasion by bacteria, then ischemia of the serosal surface
Embolus to the superior mesenteric artery, then mucosal infarction
approach: An irreducible hernia is incarcerated. Fever, tenderness, and a high lactate mean the trapped bowel has lost its blood supply, so it is strangulated.
The narrow neck of the sac squeezes the mesentery. Thin-walled, low-pressure veins collapse before thick-walled arteries do.
Blood keeps flowing in but cannot leave, so the loop swells until tissue pressure exceeds arterial pressure and the bowel infarcts.
questions.why: In an incarcerated hernia, the neck of the sac first compresses the mesenteric veins. Venous outflow stops while arterial inflow continues, so the loop becomes congested and edematous. The swelling tightens the loop in the neck even more until arterial inflow fails. The result is a hemorrhagic infarct, which is why strangulated bowel looks dark red to black. Gangrene then allows bacteria to cross the wall, causing peritonitis and sepsis.
whyNot: Arteries have thick walls and high pressure, so they are compressed last. The narrow neck squeezes the low-pressure veins first, which is why the loop became congested and edematous before it infarcted.
Correct.
Bacteria cross the wall after ischemia has damaged the mucosal barrier. They follow ischemia and are a late step in strangulation.
An embolus to the superior mesenteric artery infarcts long segments of small bowel and right colon. It does not explain a single loop trapped in a groin sac.

questions.stem: At surgery, the hernia sac lies within the internal spermatic fascia beside the ductus deferens and extends into the scrotum. Which of the following best describes the course of this sac?
options: Through the inguinal triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
Through the femoral ring, below the inguinal ligament
Through the linea semilunaris, at the level of the arcuate line
Through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
approach: A sac inside the spermatic cord coverings that reaches the scrotum followed the path of the testis through the deep ring.
The deep inguinal ring sits lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, so an indirect hernia begins lateral to them.
A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle medial to the vessels and lies outside the internal spermatic fascia.
questions.why: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the deep inguinal ring, which lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and follows the spermatic cord through the canal. It is covered by the same layers as the cord, including internal spermatic fascia, and can reach the scrotum. It often reflects a patent processus vaginalis. A direct hernia bulges through the weak posterior wall of the canal in Hesselbach triangle, bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, and the inguinal ligament.
whyNot: This is the path of a direct hernia. It bulges through the posterior wall of the canal and usually stays outside the internal spermatic fascia, so it rarely reaches the scrotum.
This is a femoral hernia. It passes below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein, and presents in the upper thigh.
This is a Spigelian hernia through the semilunar line on the anterior abdominal wall. It does not travel with the spermatic cord.
Correct.

questions.stem: The loop of ileum could slide into the hernia sac because it is suspended from the posterior abdominal wall by a mesentery. Which of the following segments of the gastrointestinal tract has the same relationship to the peritoneum as the ileum?
options: Transverse colon
Descending colon
Ascending colon
Second part of the duodenum
approach: An organ with a mesentery is intraperitoneal and mobile.
Recall the retroperitoneal gut: duodenum parts 2 to 4, ascending and descending colon, and part of the rectum. These are fixed to the posterior wall.
The transverse colon hangs on the transverse mesocolon, so it is intraperitoneal like the ileum.
questions.why: Intraperitoneal organs are wrapped in visceral peritoneum and attached by a mesentery, which lets them move. The jejunum, ileum, transverse colon, and sigmoid colon all have mesenteries, so they can enter hernia sacs or twist. Secondarily retroperitoneal structures, such as the ascending and descending colon and most of the duodenum, lost their mesentery during development and are fixed to the posterior abdominal wall.
whyNot: Correct.
The descending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal. Its mesentery fused with the posterior wall during development, so it is fixed in place.
The ascending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal and covered by peritoneum only on its front and sides.
The second part of the duodenum is retroperitoneal and fixed beside the head of the pancreas. Only the first part of the duodenum is partly intraperitoneal.

questions.stem: Before the loop became strangulated, contractions of the ileum proximal to the hernia were increased. Which of the following sets the maximum frequency of these contractions?
options: Spike potentials fired by the submucosal (Meissner) plexus
Migrating motor complexes released by motilin during fasting
Slow waves generated by the interstitial cells of Cajal
Vagal efferent bursts from the dorsal motor nucleus
approach: Gut smooth muscle contracts only when spike potentials ride on top of a slow wave.
Slow waves are rhythmic membrane depolarizations made by the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemakers of the gut.
So the slow-wave rate is the ceiling for contraction frequency. Nerves and hormones change how many slow waves trigger a contraction and how strong it is.
questions.why: Interstitial cells of Cajal produce slow waves at a set rate in each region, about 3 per minute in the stomach, about 12 in the duodenum, and about 8 to 9 in the terminal ileum. A contraction occurs only when a slow wave reaches threshold and triggers spike potentials, so the slow-wave rate is the maximum contraction rate. The myenteric plexus coordinates peristalsis by contracting the segment above a bolus and relaxing the segment below it. Proximal to an obstruction, this reflex is strongly driven, causing colicky pain.
whyNot: The submucosal plexus mainly controls secretion and local blood flow. It does not set the rhythm of smooth muscle contraction.
Motilin triggers the migrating motor complex every 90 to 120 minutes during fasting to sweep debris along. It does not set the minute-to-minute contraction rate.
Correct.
Vagal input changes the strength of contractions through the enteric nervous system, but the gut keeps its slow-wave rhythm even after vagotomy.

topics: Slow waves and interstitial cells of Cajal

dx: Ileocolic intussusception with a Meckel diverticulum lead point
case: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of 12 hours of episodes of severe abdominal pain during which he cries and draws his knees to his chest. Between episodes he is lethargic. He has vomited four times and has passed one stool of dark red blood mixed with mucus. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mmHg. Physical examination shows a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a target sign. Air enema reduction fails. At surgery, the terminal ileum has telescoped into the cecum and ascending colon, with an inverted Meckel diverticulum at its tip. The diagnosis is ileocolic intussusception with a Meckel diverticulum lead point.

questions.stem: Histologic examination of the resected diverticulum shows only ileal-type mucosa. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the dark red, mucoid stool?
options: Acid from ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerating the adjacent ileum
Shiga toxin destroying the epithelial cells of the colonic mucosa
Rupture of dilated submucosal vessels in the wall of the cecum
Venous congestion of the intussusceptum from trapped mesentery
approach: The biopsy rules out ectopic gastric mucosa as the bleeding source.
In intussusception, the inner segment (intussusceptum) pulls its mesentery in with it, and the outer segment squeezes that mesentery.
Veins are compressed first, so the inner bowel becomes congested, edematous, and ischemic. Its mucosa sloughs and releases blood and mucus, giving currant jelly stool.
questions.why: Intussusception is telescoping of one bowel segment into the next, most often ileocolic in young children. A lead point, such as hypertrophied Peyer patches after a viral illness or a Meckel diverticulum in an older child, is pulled forward by peristalsis. The mesentery of the inner segment is trapped, so venous outflow stops, and the mucosa becomes congested and ischemic. Blood mixed with mucus from the sloughing mucosa produces currant jelly stool. Without reduction, the segment infarcts. Volvulus differs because the bowel twists on its mesentery, as in sigmoid volvulus in older adults or midgut volvulus with malrotation in infants.
whyNot: Ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel diverticulum causes painless bleeding from an ulcer in nearby ileum. This diverticulum had no gastric mucosa, and his bleeding came with colicky pain.
Shiga toxin from EHEC causes bloody diarrhea and can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome. It does not cause a palpable mass or a target sign.
Dilated, fragile submucosal vessels (angiodysplasia) bleed painlessly in older adults. They are not a cause of bleeding in a child with intussusception.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the origin and wall structure of the lesion that served as this patient's lead point?
options: False diverticulum of mucosa herniating where vasa recta enter
True diverticulum from a persistent vitelline duct
Duplication cyst from failed recanalization of the ileum
Patent urachus joining the ileum to the bladder dome
approach: A Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, which joins the midgut to the yolk sac in the embryo.
The duct normally obliterates early in development. If its intestinal end persists, it forms an outpouching on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.
Because it is a remnant of the whole gut tube, it contains all layers of the wall, so it is a true diverticulum.
questions.why: Meckel diverticulum is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. It is a true diverticulum containing mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis, on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. The rule of twos describes it: about 2% of people, about 2 feet (60 cm) from the ileocecal valve, about 2 inches long, often with 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic), and usually symptomatic by age 2. It presents as painless rectal bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa, or as obstruction when it acts as a lead point for intussusception or a band for volvulus.
whyNot: False diverticula of mucosa and submucosa form where vasa recta pierce the muscle, as in sigmoid diverticulosis in older adults. They lack a muscle layer.
Correct.
Duplication cysts are rare tubular or cystic structures attached to the mesenteric side of the bowel. They are not remnants of the vitelline duct.
The urachus is the allantois remnant joining the bladder to the umbilicus. A patent urachus leaks urine at the umbilicus and has no link to the ileum.

topics: Meckel diverticulum and the rule of twos

questions.stem: At the onset of his illness, the pain was dull and poorly localized around the umbilicus. Which of the following best explains this location?
options: Foregut structure supplied by the celiac trunk, with afferents to about T5 to T9
Hindgut structure supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery, with afferents to about L1 to L2
Midgut structure supplied by the superior mesenteric artery, with afferents to about T10
Parietal peritoneum supplied by somatic intercostal nerves, with afferents to about T12
approach: Identify the involved bowel: terminal ileum, cecum, and ascending colon.
These are midgut derivatives, supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
Visceral afferents from the midgut enter the cord at about T10, so the pain is felt in the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus.
questions.why: Visceral pain fibers travel back with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at the levels that supplied the embryonic gut segment. Pain is then referred to the dermatomes of those levels. Foregut pain (to the second part of the duodenum, celiac trunk) is felt in the epigastrium. Midgut pain (to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon, superior mesenteric artery) is felt around the umbilicus. Hindgut pain (inferior mesenteric artery) is felt in the suprapubic region. Visceral pain is dull and poorly localized because the gut is innervated on both sides of the midline by few afferent fibers.
whyNot: The foregut ends at the second part of the duodenum. Its pain is felt in the epigastrium, and none of this boy's involved bowel is foregut.
The hindgut begins at the distal third of the transverse colon. Its pain is felt in the suprapubic region.
Correct.
Parietal peritoneum gives sharp, well-localized somatic pain over the inflamed area. It explains sharp, localized pain later in an illness. His early pain was dull and central.

questions.stem: During the same week, his 10-month-old sister develops vomiting and profuse watery diarrhea during a winter outbreak at her day care center. Stool testing identifies a nonenveloped virus with a segmented, double-stranded RNA genome. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her diarrhea?
options: Loss of villus-tip enterocytes, with villus blunting and malabsorption
ADP-ribosylation of Gs protein, raising enterocyte cAMP and chloride loss
Invasion of colonic mucosa through M cells, with ulceration and bleeding
Inactivation of the 60S ribosomal subunit in colonic epithelial cells
approach: Identify the virus: nonenveloped, segmented double-stranded RNA, infant, winter, day care. This is rotavirus.
Rotavirus infects the mature absorptive enterocytes at the tips of small intestinal villi.
Loss of these cells blunts villi and reduces absorption and disaccharidase activity, so fluid and unabsorbed sugar stay in the lumen. The viral protein NSP4 also increases secretion.
questions.why: Rotavirus, a reovirus with a segmented double-stranded RNA genome, is the classic cause of severe watery diarrhea in infants and young children, especially in winter. It kills mature enterocytes at the villus tips, which blunts the villi and leaves immature crypt cells that absorb poorly. Its NSP4 protein acts as an enterotoxin that raises intracellular calcium and chloride secretion. Norovirus, a single-stranded RNA calicivirus, causes outbreaks in all ages, and the enteroviruses (coxsackievirus, echovirus) are single-stranded RNA picornaviruses spread by the fecal-oral route.
whyNot: Correct.
This is the mechanism of cholera toxin and the heat-labile toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli, which are bacteria. It does not describe a double-stranded RNA virus.
M cell invasion with mucosal ulceration describes Shigella and invasive bacteria, which cause bloody diarrhea with fever.
Ribosome inactivation is the action of Shiga toxin and Shiga-like toxin. It causes bloody diarrhea. Her illness is watery and viral.

topics: Comparison of viral causes of enteritis

case: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of worsening constipation and abdominal distension. She had normal bowel habits until 8 years ago and now has a bowel movement once every 2 to 3 weeks. She grew up in a rural area of Bolivia in a house with an adobe and thatch roof and moved to the United States 10 years ago. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 62/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 122/76 mmHg. Physical examination shows a distended, tympanitic abdomen. An electrocardiogram shows right bundle branch block. Abdominal radiograph shows a massively dilated sigmoid colon and rectum. Serologic testing is positive for IgG antibodies against Trypanosoma cruzi. The diagnosis is megacolon caused by chronic Chagas disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms most likely underlies this patient's megacolon?
options: Acquired inflammatory destruction of enteric ganglion cells
Congenital absence of ganglion cells from a RET mutation
Transmural colitis with cytokine-mediated loss of muscle tone
Mechanical blockage by a stenosing rectal adenocarcinoma
approach: Normal bowel function for decades, followed by slowly progressive constipation, means the problem was acquired.
Childhood in an area with triatomine bugs, positive T. cruzi serology, and a conduction block point to chronic Chagas disease.
In chronic Chagas disease, parasite-driven inflammation destroys enteric neurons, especially in the myenteric plexus, so the colon cannot propel stool and dilates.
questions.why: Trypanosoma cruzi is spread by triatomine (reduviid) bugs in rural Latin America. Years after infection, parasite persistence and immune-mediated inflammation destroy neurons of the enteric plexuses and the cardiac conduction system. Loss of enteric neurons causes megaesophagus and megacolon, and cardiac involvement causes dilated cardiomyopathy and conduction blocks such as right bundle branch block. Hirschsprung disease differs because ganglion cells are absent from birth, so symptoms start in the newborn. Toxic megacolon differs because it is an acute, life-threatening dilation during severe colitis.
whyNot: Correct.
This is Hirschsprung disease. It presents in the newborn with delayed passage of meconium, which does not fit normal bowel habits until middle age.
This describes toxic megacolon, an acute complication of ulcerative colitis or C. difficile colitis with fever and systemic toxicity. Her course is slow and painless.
A rectal cancer can cause obstruction and proximal dilation, but the dilated segment here includes the rectum itself, and serology explains the cause.

questions.stem: Her physician contrasts her disease with Hirschsprung disease, in which the aganglionic segment always begins at the anus and extends a variable distance proximally. Which of the following best explains this distribution in Hirschsprung disease?
options: Rectal neurons arise from sacral somites, which fail to form in the embryo
Rectal ganglion cells degenerate after birth from ischemia
Neural crest cells migrate craniocaudally and reach the rectum last
Endoderm of the cloaca fails to form the intrinsic enteric plexuses
approach: Enteric neurons and glia come from neural crest cells, mainly vagal neural crest.
These cells enter the foregut and migrate down the gut in a craniocaudal direction, so the rectum is colonized last.
If migration stops early (most often from a loss-of-function RET mutation), the most distal bowel is left without ganglion cells, in one continuous segment from the anus upward.
questions.why: Vagal neural crest cells enter the foregut and migrate toward the hindgut during the embryonic period, forming the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. RET, a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by GDNF, drives their survival and migration. When migration stops short, the distal colon and rectum lack ganglion cells. The aganglionic segment stays contracted and acts as a functional obstruction, so the normal bowel above it dilates. This is why the rectum is always involved and why the defect extends proximally in one continuous segment.
whyNot: Somites form muscle, bone, and dermis of the body wall. Enteric neurons do not come from somites.
Ganglion cells in Hirschsprung disease never arrived, so they are absent at birth. There is no postnatal degeneration.
Correct.
Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the gut. Enteric neurons come from neural crest, which is ectoderm.

topics: Neural crest origin of enteric neurons

questions.stem: Anorectal manometry shows that balloon distension of her rectum fails to cause relaxation of the internal anal sphincter. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Injury to the pudendal nerve that supplies the external sphincter
Loss of intramural neurons mediating internal sphincter relaxation
Increased sympathetic tone carried by the lumbar splanchnic nerves
Fibrosis of the levator ani muscle that limits pelvic floor descent
approach: Rectal distension normally triggers reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter (the rectoanal inhibitory reflex).
This reflex runs through intrinsic enteric neurons in the wall of the rectum and sphincter, which release nitric oxide and VIP.
Chagas disease destroys those neurons, so the reflex is lost, just as it is in Hirschsprung disease.
questions.why: Defecation begins when stool stretches the rectal wall. Enteric neurons then relax the internal anal sphincter, which is smooth muscle, and the urge to defecate is felt. The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control through the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4), so a person can delay defecation. The gastrocolic reflex increases colonic motility after a meal. Loss of the intrinsic neurons removes internal sphincter relaxation, so stool cannot pass easily and the colon above dilates.
whyNot: Pudendal nerve injury weakens the external sphincter and causes incontinence. It does not affect reflex relaxation of the internal sphincter.
Correct.
Sympathetic input raises internal sphincter tone, but it does not abolish the intrinsic relaxation reflex. Chagas disease destroys the enteric neurons that run that reflex.
Levator ani dysfunction can cause dyssynergic defecation, but this muscle is skeletal and does not control the internal sphincter's reflex relaxation.

topics: Defecation reflex and rectoanal inhibitory reflex

questions.stem: A biopsy is planned to examine the neural plexus that coordinates contraction of the muscular coat of her colon. Which of the following locations must the tissue sample include?
options: Lamina propria directly beneath the surface epithelium
Between the muscularis mucosae and the inner circular muscle
Between the outer longitudinal muscle and the serosa
Between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers
approach: The plexus that controls motility of the muscular wall is the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.
It sits in the muscularis externa, between its inner circular and outer longitudinal layers.
A superficial suction biopsy reaches only mucosa and submucosa, so a full-thickness sample is needed to see this plexus.
questions.why: The gut wall has mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa or adventitia. The submucosal (Meissner) plexus lies in the submucosa and mainly regulates secretion and blood flow. The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa and controls motility. In Chagas disease the myenteric plexus is the main target, which is why motility fails.
whyNot: The lamina propria contains capillaries, lymphocytes, and lymphatics. It does not contain either enteric plexus.
This is the submucosa, which holds the submucosal (Meissner) plexus. That plexus mainly controls secretion and local blood flow.
The tissue between the longitudinal muscle and serosa is subserosal connective tissue. No major enteric plexus lies there.
Correct.

topics: Location of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses

case: A 74-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive difficulty swallowing. He often regurgitates undigested food that he ate several hours earlier, and his wife reports bad breath. He notices a gurgling sound in his neck when he drinks and has had nighttime coughing spells. He has lost 5 kg (11 lb) over this period. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 136/82 mmHg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A barium swallow shows a contrast-filled pouch extending posteriorly from the pharynx just above the cricopharyngeus muscle. The diagnosis is Zenker diverticulum.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains the formation of this patient's pouch?
options: Traction on the full esophageal wall by scarred mediastinal lymph nodes
Persistent embryonic connection between the foregut and the trachea
Pulsion of mucosa through a weak area above a poorly relaxing sphincter
Failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation from loss of inhibitory neurons
approach: Locate the pouch: posterior hypopharynx, just above the cricopharyngeus, in Killian triangle.
The cricopharyngeus (upper esophageal sphincter) does not open fully during swallowing, so pressure in the hypopharynx rises.
Over years, that pressure pushes mucosa and submucosa out through the weak area. This is a false (pulsion) diverticulum.
questions.why: Zenker diverticulum forms in Killian triangle, a weak area of the posterior pharyngeal wall between the thyropharyngeal part of the inferior constrictor and the cricopharyngeus. Poor relaxation of the cricopharyngeus raises pressure during each swallow, and mucosa and submucosa bulge out without a muscle layer. Food collects in the pouch, causing dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, gurgling, and aspiration. It occurs mostly in older adults.
whyNot: Traction diverticula form in the midesophagus when scarred lymph nodes (for example after tuberculosis or histoplasmosis) pull out all layers of the wall. They are true diverticula and usually cause no symptoms.
A persistent foregut to trachea connection is a tracheoesophageal fistula, a congenital defect that presents in newborns with choking and feeding problems.
Correct.
This is achalasia. It affects the lower esophageal sphincter and causes a dilated esophagus above a narrow distal segment, far below this pouch.

questions.stem: In a normal swallow, the muscle at the lower edge of this patient's pouch relaxes to let the bolus pass. Which of the following best describes the phase of swallowing in which this occurs and how it is controlled?
options: Voluntary oral phase controlled by the motor cortex
Esophageal phase controlled by the myenteric plexus alone
Esophageal phase controlled by vagal nitric oxide release
Reflex pharyngeal phase coordinated by the medulla
approach: The muscle below the pouch is the cricopharyngeus, which forms the upper esophageal sphincter.
It relaxes when the bolus reaches the pharynx, during the involuntary pharyngeal phase.
That phase is a reflex triggered by touch receptors in the pharynx and run by the swallowing center in the medulla through cranial nerves IX and X.
questions.why: Chewing uses the muscles of mastication, supplied by CN V3. Swallowing then begins with a voluntary oral phase in which the tongue pushes the bolus back. When the bolus touches the pharynx, the pharyngeal phase starts as a reflex coordinated by the medullary swallowing center. The soft palate closes the nasopharynx, the larynx rises and the epiglottis covers it, breathing stops, and the upper esophageal sphincter relaxes. In the esophageal phase, peristalsis carries the bolus down, and vagal fibers that release nitric oxide and VIP relax the lower esophageal sphincter and proximal stomach.
whyNot: The oral phase moves the bolus to the back of the mouth and is voluntary. Opening of the upper esophageal sphincter happens after it, as a reflex.
The myenteric plexus helps run peristalsis in the smooth muscle of the lower esophagus. The cricopharyngeus is skeletal muscle controlled from the brainstem.
Vagal nitric oxide relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter at the end of the esophagus. The pouch sits at the upper sphincter.
Correct.

questions.stem: During surgery, a biopsy specimen is taken from the lining of the pouch. Which of the following types of epithelium is most likely to be seen?
options: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium with many goblet cells
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
approach: The pouch is a false diverticulum, so its lining is the mucosa of the area it came from.
It arises from the hypopharynx just above the esophagus.
The hypopharynx and esophagus are lined by moist, nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium that resists abrasion from food.
questions.why: The oropharynx, hypopharynx, and esophagus carry rough food boluses, so they are lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium kept moist by mucous glands. The stomach and intestines are lined by simple columnar epithelium for secretion and absorption. The anal canal is columnar above the pectinate line and stratified squamous below it. Because the pouch is mucosa pushed out of the hypopharynx, it keeps the same squamous lining.
whyNot: Keratinized epithelium covers dry surfaces such as skin and the hard palate. The pharynx and esophagus are normally nonkeratinized.
Correct.
Columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines the intestine. In the esophagus it appears only as Barrett metaplasia near the gastroesophageal junction.
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium lines the nasopharynx and airways. The hypopharynx, where this pouch arises, is a food passage with squamous lining.

questions.stem: An endoscope passed into this patient's esophagus would meet a natural narrowing just below the opening of the pouch. Which of the following best describes this narrowing and its approximate vertebral level?
options: Cricopharyngeus muscle at about C6
Thoracic inlet behind the manubrium at about T1
Aortic arch and left main bronchus at about T4 to T5
Esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm at about T10
approach: The pouch arises just above the cricopharyngeus, so the narrowing below its opening is the start of the esophagus.
The esophagus begins at the cricopharyngeus at about the level of C6 and the cricoid cartilage.
The other two narrowings are where the aortic arch and left main bronchus cross it and where it passes through the diaphragm at T10.
questions.why: The esophagus begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, about C6, where the cricopharyngeus forms the upper esophageal sphincter. It descends through the superior and posterior mediastinum and has three natural narrowings: at the cricopharyngeus, where the aortic arch and then the left main bronchus cross it, and at the esophageal hiatus at T10. These are the sites where swallowed objects tend to lodge and where an endoscope meets resistance. The cricopharyngeal narrowing is the tightest, and a Zenker pouch sits just above it.
whyNot: Correct.
The thoracic inlet is the opening at the top of the thorax. It is not one of the three classic esophageal narrowings.
This is the middle (thoracic) narrowing, well below the neck. The pouch arises in the neck.
This is the lowest narrowing where the esophagus enters the abdomen. It is far below the pouch.

topics: Course and narrowings of the esophagus

case: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of 6 to 8 watery, nonbloody stools daily, including at night, with mild crampy abdominal pain and a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight loss. She takes naproxen daily for osteoarthritis of the knees. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Hemoglobin concentration is 13.1 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0), and C-reactive protein is 3 mg/L (below 10). Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile toxin is negative. Serum IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are negative with a normal total IgA. Colonoscopy shows normal-appearing mucosa throughout. Biopsy specimens confirm collagenous colitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is most likely to be seen on this patient's colonic biopsy specimens?
options: Crypt abscesses with crypt distortion and basal plasmacytosis
Thickened collagen band beneath the surface epithelium
Noncaseating granulomas with transmural lymphoid aggregates
Hyalinized small vessels with atypical stromal fibroblasts
approach: Chronic watery diarrhea with a normal-looking colon at colonoscopy points to microscopic colitis.
Microscopic colitis has two forms. The collagenous form has a thick subepithelial collagen band (over about 10 µm), and the lymphocytic form has excess intraepithelial lymphocytes without the band.
Collagenous colitis also has more intraepithelial lymphocytes and lamina propria inflammation, but the collagen band defines it.
questions.why: Microscopic colitis causes chronic, nonbloody watery diarrhea, often nocturnal, mostly in middle-aged and older women. The colon looks normal, so the diagnosis needs biopsies. Collagenous colitis shows a collagen band under the surface epithelium thicker than about 10 µm, with surface damage and inflammation in the lamina propria. It is linked to autoimmune disease, celiac disease, and drugs such as NSAIDs and proton pump inhibitors. Other noninfectious causes of colitis include radiation and NSAID injury.
whyNot: Crypt abscesses with crypt architectural distortion and basal plasmacytosis are features of ulcerative colitis. That disease causes bloody diarrhea and visible mucosal inflammation.
Correct.
Noncaseating granulomas and transmural inflammation define Crohn disease, which usually shows ulcers or strictures on colonoscopy.
Hyalinized vessels and atypical fibroblasts are features of chronic radiation injury. Nothing in her history suggests radiation therapy.

questions.stem: Before colonoscopy, irritable bowel syndrome was included in the differential diagnosis. Which of the following features of this patient's presentation most strongly argued against that diagnosis?
options: Nocturnal bowel movements and weight loss
Cramping abdominal pain that eases after defecation
Loose stools that have persisted for several months
Normal hemoglobin and C-reactive protein levels
approach: Irritable bowel syndrome is recurrent abdominal pain linked to defecation, with a change in stool frequency or form, and no structural disease.
Its symptoms come from altered motility and visceral hypersensitivity during waking hours, so they do not wake the patient from sleep and do not cause weight loss.
Nocturnal diarrhea and weight loss are alarm features that point to organic disease and call for further testing.
questions.why: Irritable bowel syndrome is a disorder of gut and brain interaction. Altered motility, visceral hypersensitivity, and changes in central pain processing cause recurrent pain that is related to defecation, with altered stool form. There is no inflammation or structural lesion. Diarrhea that wakes a patient at night, weight loss, bleeding, anemia, and onset after age 50 are alarm features that suggest an organic cause such as microscopic colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, or cancer. Gastroparesis, a motility disorder with measurably delayed gastric emptying, causes early satiety and vomiting from delayed gastric emptying, usually from diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
whyNot: Correct.
Pain that improves after defecation is one of the core features of irritable bowel syndrome, so it supports that diagnosis.
Irritable bowel syndrome is defined by symptoms lasting months, so chronic loose stools fit it.
Normal blood counts and inflammatory markers are expected in irritable bowel syndrome, so they support that diagnosis.

topics: Irritable bowel syndrome and alarm features

questions.stem: Celiac disease was considered because it is associated with microscopic colitis. In a patient with celiac disease, which of the following steps allows dietary gliadin peptides to activate the T-cell response in the small intestine?
options: Presentation of native gliadin on HLA-B27 to CD8 T cells
Cross-linking of IgE on mucosal mast cells by gliadin peptides
Activation of the classical complement pathway by bound gliadin
Tissue transglutaminase deamidation for HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 binding
approach: Gliadin, from wheat gluten, is rich in proline and glutamine, so it resists digestion and crosses the epithelium as long peptides.
Tissue transglutaminase in the lamina propria converts some glutamines to glutamate (deamidation), adding negative charges.
These charged peptides bind tightly to HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 on antigen-presenting cells, which activate gluten-specific CD4 T cells.
questions.why: Celiac disease needs gluten, the right HLA class II genes, and tissue transglutaminase. Deamidated gliadin binds HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 strongly and is presented to CD4 T cells, which release interferon-gamma and drive villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Gliadin bound to tissue transglutaminase also helps B cells make IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase and endomysium, which are the screening tests. Because selective IgA deficiency is more common in celiac disease and can cause a false negative IgA test, total IgA is checked at the same time.
whyNot: HLA-B27 is a class I allele linked to the seronegative spondyloarthropathies. Celiac disease is linked to the class II alleles HLA-DQ2 and DQ8.
IgE cross-linking on mast cells causes wheat allergy, an immediate hypersensitivity with hives or anaphylaxis. Celiac disease is a T cell-mediated disorder.
Complement activation is not the driver of celiac disease. The injury comes from gluten-specific CD4 T cells and cytotoxic intraepithelial lymphocytes.
Correct.

questions.stem: Stool was tested for C. difficile toxin because she had received clindamycin for a dental infection 6 weeks before her symptoms began. If C. difficile had been the cause, which of the following mechanisms would have produced her diarrhea?
options: Heat-stable toxin activating guanylate cyclase in enterocytes
Preformed superantigen toxin acting on the vagal afferents
Toxins A and B inactivating Rho GTPases of colonocytes
Spread between enterocytes by polymerizing host actin
approach: Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins suppress normal colonic flora, which lets C. difficile spores germinate and grow.
C. difficile makes toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin).
Both toxins glucosylate Rho family GTPases, which breaks down the actin cytoskeleton, opens tight junctions, kills colonocytes, and triggers inflammation.
questions.why: C. difficile is a spore-forming, anaerobic gram-positive rod. After antibiotics disrupt the normal flora, it grows in the colon and releases toxins A and B. These toxins inactivate Rho GTPases, so colonocytes lose their cytoskeleton and tight junctions and die. Neutrophils, fibrin, and mucus erupt from damaged crypts and form yellow-white pseudomembranes. Patients have watery diarrhea, cramps, and fever, and severe cases can progress to toxic megacolon. Diagnosis is by stool toxin testing or by PCR for the toxin genes.
whyNot: Heat-stable toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli raises cGMP and causes traveler's diarrhea. It does not cause antibiotic-associated colitis.
Preformed Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxins cause vomiting within hours of eating contaminated food. They do not cause weeks of diarrhea after antibiotics.
Correct.
Actin-based spread between cells is used by Listeria and Shigella. C. difficile does not invade cells; it damages them with toxins from the lumen.

topics: Clostridioides difficile toxins and pseudomembranous colitis

case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 3 days of abdominal pain. The pain began around the umbilicus and moved to the right lower quadrant within a day. She did not seek care until fever and nausea developed. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg. Physical examination shows right lower quadrant tenderness with guarding. Rectal examination shows tenderness anteriorly. Leukocyte count is 18,200/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000) with 88% neutrophils (40 to 70). A urine pregnancy test is negative. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis shows a dilated appendix with an appendicolith, periappendiceal fat stranding, and a 5-cm rim-enhancing fluid collection in the pelvis. The diagnosis is perforated acute appendicitis with a pelvic abscess.

questions.stem: Which of the following sequences of events best explains how the appendicolith led to perforation in this patient?
options: Viral ulceration of the mucosa, then fibrosis with a stricture
Bacterial invasion of the wall, then lymphoid hyperplasia
Arterial thrombosis, then mucosal necrosis and stone formation
Luminal obstruction, rising pressure, ischemia, then invasion
approach: Start with the appendicolith. It blocks the lumen of a narrow, blind-ended tube.
Mucus keeps being secreted, so pressure rises. Veins collapse first, then arterial flow falls, and the wall becomes ischemic.
Ischemic mucosa lets luminal bacteria invade the wall, causing suppurative inflammation, gangrene, and perforation.
questions.why: Appendicitis usually starts with obstruction of the lumen by a fecalith or by lymphoid hyperplasia after an infection. Continued secretion raises pressure, which blocks venous outflow and then arterial inflow. Ischemia lets bacteria invade the wall, producing neutrophilic inflammation through the muscularis. Early pain is visceral and felt around the umbilicus. When inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, pain localizes to McBurney point. Untreated, the gangrenous wall can perforate, causing an abscess or peritonitis.
whyNot: Viral illness can cause lymphoid hyperplasia that blocks the lumen, but mucosal ulceration followed by fibrosis does not describe acute appendicitis.
This reverses the order. Lymphoid hyperplasia can be a first step that blocks the lumen, and bacterial invasion comes after ischemia.
Fecaliths form from hardened stool before the illness. Arterial thrombosis is not the first event in appendicitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: At laparoscopy, the inflamed appendix is hidden by adhesions behind the cecum. Which of the following landmarks most reliably leads the surgeon to the base of the appendix?
options: Line of omental appendices along the ascending colon
Deepest haustral fold of the cecal wall
Convergence point of the three taeniae coli
Last Peyer patch on the antimesenteric ileum
approach: The tip of the appendix can lie in many places (retrocecal, pelvic, subcecal), but its base is fixed on the cecum.
The three taeniae coli are bands of longitudinal muscle on the colon.
Followed down the cecum, they converge at the base of the appendix, where they become its continuous longitudinal muscle layer.
questions.why: The colon differs from the small intestine by its taeniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices (fat tags). The taeniae are three bands of the outer longitudinal muscle. They meet at the base of the appendix, which on the skin surface lies near McBurney point, one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. Because the tip of the appendix varies in position, following the taeniae is the reliable way to find the base.
whyNot: Omental appendices are fat tags along the colon. They help identify colon but do not point to the appendix, and the appendix itself lacks them.
Haustra are sacculations of the colon wall between taeniae. They change with contraction and do not mark the appendix base.
Correct.
Peyer patches are lymphoid follicles in the ileal mucosa on the antimesenteric side. They are not visible from the outside and do not lead to the appendix.

topics: Features of the colon versus small intestine

questions.stem: The same month, her 15-year-old brother undergoes surgery for suspected appendicitis. At surgery, the appendix is normal, but the terminal ileum is thickened and the mesenteric lymph nodes are enlarged. Stool culture grows a gram-negative coccobacillus that grows well after cold enrichment at 4 °C (39.2 °F). Which of the following exposures most likely caused his infection?
options: Eating undercooked ground beef at a picnic
Preparing raw pork chitterlings at home
Eating fried rice left at room temperature
Eating raw oysters harvested in summer
approach: A gram-negative organism that grows in the cold and causes terminal ileitis with mesenteric adenitis is Yersinia enterocolitica.
It invades through M cells over Peyer patches and spreads to mesenteric lymph nodes, causing right lower quadrant pain that mimics appendicitis.
Its main reservoir is pigs, so pork products, especially chitterlings, and unpasteurized milk are typical sources.
questions.why: Yersinia enterocolitica is a gram-negative coccobacillus that can grow at refrigerator temperatures. It crosses the ileal mucosa through M cells, multiplies in Peyer patches, and spreads to mesenteric lymph nodes. The result is fever, diarrhea, and right lower quadrant pain from mesenteric adenitis, a pseudoappendicitis that can lead to surgery. Pigs are the main reservoir, and handling raw chitterlings is a classic source, along with contaminated milk.
whyNot: Undercooked ground beef is the classic source of EHEC O157:H7, which makes Shiga toxin and causes bloody diarrhea that can progress to hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Correct.

Fried rice left at room temperature is the classic source of Bacillus cereus, a gram-positive rod whose preformed toxin causes vomiting within hours. It does not cause terminal ileitis or mesenteric adenitis.
Raw oysters carry Vibrio species, which are curved gram-negative rods linked to warm seawater. They do not cause mesenteric adenitis.

questions.stem: The abscess formed while she was mostly sitting and walking during the days before admission. In which of the following peritoneal spaces is this collection most likely located?
options: Rectouterine pouch
Vesicouterine pouch
Hepatorenal recess
Right subphrenic space
approach: Fluid and pus in the peritoneal cavity flow to the lowest space for the patient's position.
In an upright woman, the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity is the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) between the uterus and rectum.
This fits the CT finding of a pelvic collection and the anterior tenderness on rectal examination.
questions.why: Gravity decides where infected fluid collects. When upright, the lowest peritoneal space is the rectouterine pouch in women and the rectovesical pouch in men. When supine, the lowest space in the upper abdomen is the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch). Fluid can also track up the right paracolic gutter to the subphrenic spaces. A collection in the rectouterine pouch lies just in front of the rectum, so it causes anterior rectal tenderness and can be drained through the rectum or vagina.
whyNot: Correct.
The vesicouterine pouch between the bladder and uterus is shallow and higher than the rectouterine pouch, so fluid passes it by.
The hepatorenal recess is the most dependent upper abdominal space when a person lies supine. It lies in the upper abdomen, far above the pelvis.
The subphrenic spaces lie under the diaphragm. Pus reaches them by tracking up the paracolic gutters, and they are not pelvic.

case: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of 15 years of heartburn and regurgitation that wake him at night. BMI is 33 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 134/84 mmHg. Physical examination shows central obesity and no other abnormalities. Upper endoscopy shows a small sliding hiatal hernia and salmon-colored mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastroesophageal junction into the distal esophagus. Multiple biopsy specimens are taken. Histologic examination confirms Barrett esophagus without dysplasia.

questions.stem: Surveillance endoscopy with biopsy is planned for this patient. Which of the following findings on a future biopsy would indicate the next step in the progression toward cancer?
options: Low-grade dysplasia in the columnar epithelium
Gastric cardiac-type mucosa without goblet cells
At least 15 eosinophils per high-power field in the squamous mucosa
Basal cell hyperplasia of the remaining squamous mucosa
approach: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia, which is the first step in the sequence toward esophageal adenocarcinoma.
The sequence runs from metaplasia to low-grade dysplasia, then high-grade dysplasia, then invasive adenocarcinoma.
Surveillance biopsies look for dysplasia, which is the next step and the main predictor of cancer risk.
questions.why: Chronic acid and bile reflux injures the squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus. It heals with columnar epithelium containing goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), which resists acid better. Over years, the metaplastic cells can gain genetic changes, such as TP53 mutation, that lead to low-grade and then high-grade dysplasia and finally adenocarcinoma. The risk of cancer rises with the grade of dysplasia, which is why patients with Barrett esophagus have endoscopic surveillance with biopsies.
whyNot: Correct.
Columnar mucosa without goblet cells is cardiac-type mucosa. It is a less specific finding and is not a step beyond intestinal metaplasia.
Many eosinophils in squamous mucosa define eosinophilic esophagitis, an allergic disorder. It is not part of the Barrett sequence.
Basal cell hyperplasia and elongated papillae are signs of reflux injury to squamous mucosa. They precede metaplasia and do not mark progression toward cancer.

questions.stem: Which of the following histologic findings in the salmon-colored mucosa established this patient's diagnosis?
options: Keratinized squamous cells in place of nonkeratinized ones
Columnar epithelium with goblet cells in place of squamous
Parietal and chief cells forming gastric glands in the submucosa
Atypical squamous cells extending into the lamina propria
approach: Know the normal lining: the esophagus has nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and the stomach starts with simple columnar epithelium at the gastroesophageal junction.
Salmon-colored mucosa above the junction means columnar epithelium has replaced the squamous lining.
Goblet cells in that columnar lining show intestinal-type metaplasia, which defines Barrett esophagus.
questions.why: The esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which looks pale pink at endoscopy. The stomach and intestine are lined by simple columnar epithelium, which looks red and velvety. Normally the two meet at the gastroesophageal junction (the Z-line). In Barrett esophagus, chronic reflux causes the distal squamous lining to be replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells, an intestinal pattern that is not normally found in the esophagus or stomach.
whyNot: Reflux does not make the esophageal lining keratinize. In Barrett esophagus the squamous lining is replaced by columnar epithelium.
Correct.
Gastric glands deep in the submucosa would be a heterotopia. Barrett esophagus is a change in the surface epithelium.
Atypical squamous cells invading the lamina propria describe squamous cell carcinoma, which is not the result of Barrett metaplasia.

topics: Epithelium of the esophagus and gastroesophageal junction

questions.stem: This patient's reflux injury depends on acid secreted by gastric parietal cells. Blocking which of the following would most completely reduce acid output regardless of the stimulus?
options: Histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells
Muscarinic M3 receptors on parietal cells
H+/K+ ATPase in the parietal cell apical membrane
Gastrin (CCK-B) receptors on enterochromaffin-like cells
approach: Parietal cells respond to three stimuli: acetylcholine (M3), gastrin (CCK-B), and histamine (H2).
Each receptor acts through its own second messenger (calcium for M3 and CCK-B, cAMP for H2), so blocking one leaves the others working.
All three pathways converge on the H+/K+ ATPase, the final step that pumps H+ into the lumen in exchange for K+.
questions.why: Acid secretion has a cephalic phase (sight, smell, and taste of food acting through the vagus), a gastric phase (stretch and peptides in the stomach, which release gastrin), and an intestinal phase. Acetylcholine and gastrin raise intracellular calcium, and histamine from enterochromaffin-like cells raises cAMP. These signals move H+/K+ ATPase pumps to the apical membrane and activate them. Because every stimulus works through this pump, blocking it reduces acid output the most. Somatostatin from D cells inhibits acid secretion.
whyNot: Blocking H2 receptors removes the histamine signal and also blunts gastrin's effect, which works largely through histamine. Acetylcholine can still stimulate parietal cells directly.
Blocking M3 receptors removes vagal stimulation, mainly during the cephalic phase. Gastrin and histamine can still drive secretion.
Correct.
Blocking gastrin receptors removes one stimulus, but acetylcholine and histamine released by other signals can still drive the parietal cell.

topics: Parietal cell stimulation and the proton pump

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most likely type and location of the cancer this patient is at increased risk of developing?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the upper third
Squamous cell carcinoma of the middle third
Adenocarcinoma of the upper third
Adenocarcinoma of the distal third
approach: Barrett esophagus is glandular (columnar) metaplasia, so the cancer that follows is a glandular cancer, adenocarcinoma.
Barrett esophagus forms in the distal esophagus near the gastroesophageal junction, so the tumor arises there.
Obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure and reflux, which adds to the same risk.
questions.why: Esophageal adenocarcinoma arises from Barrett esophagus in the distal third. Its risk factors are chronic reflux, Barrett esophagus, obesity, and smoking. Squamous cell carcinoma arises in the upper and middle thirds and is linked to alcohol, tobacco, achalasia, caustic injury, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome. Both types present with progressive dysphagia, first to solids and then to liquids, with weight loss.
whyNot: Squamous cell carcinoma of the upper esophagus is linked to alcohol, tobacco, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome. It does not arise from Barrett metaplasia.
Squamous cell carcinoma most often arises in the middle third, linked to alcohol and tobacco. Barrett esophagus leads to a glandular tumor.
Adenocarcinoma follows the columnar metaplasia, which forms in the distal esophagus. The upper third keeps its squamous lining.
Correct.

topics: Esophageal adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma

dx: Angiodysplasia of the cecum with sigmoid diverticulosis
case: A 79-year-old woman comes to the physician because of three episodes of painless passage of maroon blood per rectum over the past 6 months and increasing fatigue. She also reports exertional lightheadedness. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mmHg. Physical examination shows conjunctival pallor and a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to the carotid arteries. Hemoglobin concentration is 8.6 g/dL (12.0 to 16.0), mean corpuscular volume is 72 fL (80 to 100), and serum ferritin is 8 ng/mL (15 to 200). Colonoscopy shows several small, flat, cherry-red lesions in the cecum and numerous diverticula in the sigmoid colon without inflammation. Echocardiography shows severe calcific aortic stenosis. The diagnosis is cecal angiodysplasia with sigmoid diverticulosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best links this patient's heart disease to the bleeding from her colonic lesions?
options: Antibodies against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa
Septic emboli from the valve eroding mucosal vessels
Shear-induced loss of large von Willebrand factor multimers
Vitamin K deficiency from reduced colonic bacterial synthesis
approach: Angiodysplasia with aortic stenosis is Heyde syndrome.
High-velocity, turbulent flow through the narrow valve stretches large von Willebrand factor multimers, exposing a site that ADAMTS13 cleaves.
Loss of the largest multimers reduces platelet adhesion, which matters most in fragile, thin-walled vessels such as angiodysplasias, so they bleed.
questions.why: Angiodysplasias are dilated, thin-walled, tortuous submucosal vessels, mostly in the cecum and right colon of older adults. They are thought to form when repeated contraction of the colon wall partly blocks submucosal veins, and the high wall tension of the wide cecum adds to this. They cause painless, often recurrent lower GI bleeding and iron deficiency. In aortic stenosis, shear stress causes an acquired von Willebrand syndrome, which makes the lesions bleed more. Replacing the valve often reduces the bleeding. Angiodysplasia is also linked to end-stage kidney disease.
whyNot: Antibodies against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa occur in immune thrombocytopenia, which lowers the platelet count and causes petechiae. Nothing links them to aortic stenosis.
Septic emboli come from infective endocarditis, which causes fever and vegetations. Her valve is calcified, and her lesions are vascular ectasias.
Correct.
Vitamin K deficiency raises the PT and causes bleeding from many sites. Aortic stenosis does not cause it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the outpouchings in this patient's sigmoid colon?
options: Mucosa and submucosa herniating where vasa recta pierce the muscle
All wall layers bulging at a persistent embryonic duct remnant
Dilated submucosal veins draining into the inferior mesenteric vein
Mucosal folds raised over areas of submucosal lymphoid hyperplasia
approach: Sigmoid diverticula in an older adult are acquired false diverticula.
Low-fiber diet and strong segmental contractions raise pressure in the narrow sigmoid colon.
That pressure pushes mucosa and submucosa out through weak points in the muscularis externa where the vasa recta enter the wall.
questions.why: Diverticulosis comes from high intraluminal pressure acting on weak spots in the colon wall. The sigmoid colon is the narrowest part of the colon, so segmental contractions there produce the highest pressures. Mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscularis where vasa recta penetrate it, which is why the vessel is stretched over the dome of the pouch. That vessel can rupture into the lumen and cause painless bleeding, often large. Diverticulitis is inflammation of a pouch after obstruction or microperforation and causes left lower quadrant pain, fever, abscess, or fistula.
whyNot: Correct.
A full-thickness outpouching from an embryonic duct remnant is a Meckel diverticulum, which arises from the ileum.
Dilated submucosal veins in the anal canal are hemorrhoids, and dilated vessels in the right colon are angiodysplasia. Neither forms outpouchings.
Lymphoid hyperplasia raises small nodules on the mucosa. It does not create pouches that extend outside the colon wall.

questions.stem: A month later, she has a brisk episode of bleeding. Angiography shows active extravasation of contrast from a vessel in the cecum. Which of the following arteries is the most likely source?
options: Left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery
Sigmoid branch of the inferior mesenteric artery
Middle colic branch of the superior mesenteric artery
Ileocolic branch of the superior mesenteric artery
approach: The cecum is a midgut derivative, so it is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
Among the branches of the superior mesenteric artery, the ileocolic artery supplies the terminal ileum, cecum, and appendix.
The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon, and the branches of the inferior mesenteric artery supply the distal colon.
questions.why: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, from the second part of the duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon. Its colic branches are the ileocolic (terminal ileum, cecum, appendix), right colic (ascending colon), and middle colic (transverse colon). The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the distal transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum through its left colic, sigmoid, and superior rectal branches. The marginal artery links the two systems. Its weak points, the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction, are the watershed zones for ischemic colitis.
whyNot: The left colic artery supplies the distal transverse and descending colon. It does not reach the cecum.
The sigmoid arteries supply the sigmoid colon. They would be the source if one of her sigmoid diverticula bled.
The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon. It does not supply the cecum.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the low mean corpuscular volume of this patient's erythrocytes?
options: Defective globin chain synthesis from an inherited gene mutation
Too little iron for heme synthesis, so extra divisions occur
Delayed nuclear maturation from impaired DNA synthesis
Lead inhibition of ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase
approach: Low hemoglobin, low MCV, and low ferritin together mean iron deficiency. Ferritin reflects body iron stores.
Repeated blood loss from the colon removes iron faster than the gut can absorb it, which drains her stores over months.
Without iron, the precursor cannot finish making heme and hemoglobin, so it divides extra times before maturing, and the red cells end up small and pale.
questions.why: Iron is absorbed as ferrous iron in the duodenum and is needed for the final step of heme synthesis, when ferrochelatase inserts it into protoporphyrin IX. When iron runs out, hemoglobin builds up slowly in red cell precursors, so they go through extra divisions and give rise to small, pale (microcytic, hypochromic) cells. Low ferritin separates iron deficiency from other microcytic anemias. In an older adult, iron deficiency calls for a search for gastrointestinal blood loss. Other mineral deficiencies show different findings: zinc causes poor wound healing and dysgeusia, and copper causes anemia, neutropenia, and myelopathy.
whyNot: Thalassemia causes microcytosis from reduced globin synthesis, but ferritin is normal or high. Her low ferritin shows iron deficiency.
Correct.
Impaired DNA synthesis from folate or vitamin B12 deficiency delays nuclear maturation and makes large cells (macrocytic anemia). Her cells are small.
Lead poisoning can cause microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling, but ferritin is not low, and nothing suggests lead exposure.

topics: Iron deficiency anemia from chronic GI blood loss

dx: Helicobacter pylori duodenal ulcer with bleeding
case: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of black, tarry stools for 1 day and one episode of vomiting coffee-ground material. For 3 months, he has had burning epigastric pain that improves with meals and returns 2 to 3 hours later, often waking him at night. He does not take NSAIDs. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mmHg. Hemoglobin concentration is 9.4 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5), serum urea nitrogen is 38 mg/dL (7 to 20), and serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.2). Upper endoscopy shows a 1.5-cm ulcer on the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb with a visible vessel. Antral biopsy specimens show curved bacilli in the surface mucus. The diagnosis is a bleeding Helicobacter pylori-associated duodenal ulcer.

questions.stem: Which of the following arteries is most likely the source of this patient's bleeding?
options: Left gastric artery
Gastroduodenal artery
Splenic artery
Superior mesenteric artery
approach: Locate the ulcer: posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.
The gastroduodenal artery runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum.
A posterior duodenal ulcer that erodes deeply can open this artery and cause major bleeding. An anterior ulcer is more likely to perforate and release free air.
questions.why: Peptic ulcers can bleed, perforate, or obstruct. The vessel at risk depends on the ulcer's location. A posterior duodenal bulb ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, causing hematemesis and melena. An anterior duodenal ulcer is more likely to perforate into the peritoneal cavity and cause free air under the diaphragm. An ulcer on the lesser curvature of the stomach can erode the left gastric artery. Duodenal ulcers cause pain that improves with meals and are almost never malignant, while gastric ulcer pain worsens with meals, and gastric ulcers need biopsy to exclude cancer.
whyNot: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach. It is the usual source of bleeding from lesser curvature gastric ulcers.
Correct.
The splenic artery runs along the top of the pancreas behind the stomach. A posterior gastric ulcer could erode it, but it does not lie behind the duodenum.
The superior mesenteric artery passes behind the neck of the pancreas and in front of the third part of the duodenum. It is not related to the duodenal bulb.

questions.stem: A urea breath test is used to confirm eradication of the organism after treatment. Which of the following properties of the organism allows both this test and its survival in the stomach?
options: Spore coat that resists gastric acid
Catalase that breaks down hydrogen peroxide
Polysaccharide capsule that blocks phagocytosis
Urease that converts urea to ammonia and CO2
approach: In the breath test, the patient swallows urea labeled with carbon-13 or carbon-14.
If H. pylori is present, its urease splits the urea into ammonia and labeled CO2, which is absorbed and breathed out.
The same ammonia buffers acid around the organism, letting it survive in the mucus layer.
questions.why: Helicobacter pylori is a curved, flagellated, microaerophilic gram-negative rod. Its flagella let it swim into the mucus layer, and its urease makes ammonia that neutralizes acid around it. Urease also explains the diagnostic tests: the urea breath test and the rapid urease test on biopsy tissue. Stool antigen testing and biopsy with histology or culture also detect it. The breath test and stool antigen detect active infection, so they are used to confirm eradication.
whyNot: H. pylori does not form spores. Spore-forming bacteria include Bacillus and Clostridium species.
H. pylori is catalase positive, but catalase protects against oxidants. It does not neutralize acid or produce the labeled CO2 measured in the test.
A capsule helps bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae avoid phagocytosis. It does not protect against acid or explain the breath test.
Correct.

questions.stem: Infection of this patient's gastric antrum increases the acid load delivered to his duodenum. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this increase?
options: Reduced somatostatin from antral D cells, releasing gastrin
Destruction of parietal cells in the gastric body and fundus
Increased secretin release from duodenal S cells
Autonomous gastrin secretion by a pancreatic tumor
approach: Normally, acid in the antrum stimulates D cells to release somatostatin, which inhibits gastrin release from G cells.
Antral-predominant H. pylori gastritis damages D cells, so somatostatin falls.
Gastrin is no longer held back, so parietal cells secrete more acid, and more acid reaches the duodenum.
questions.why: Somatostatin is the main brake on acid secretion. It acts locally on G cells, enterochromaffin-like cells, and parietal cells. When H. pylori infects the antrum, it reduces D cells and somatostatin, so gastrin and acid output rise. The excess acid entering the duodenum causes gastric metaplasia there, which H. pylori can then colonize, and the duodenal mucosa ulcerates. Infection centered in the gastric body has the opposite effect, causing atrophy and low acid.
whyNot: Correct.
Destruction of parietal cells lowers acid output. This happens in autoimmune gastritis and in H. pylori gastritis centered in the gastric body.
Secretin is released by acid in the duodenum. It stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate and inhibits gastrin, so it lowers acid.
A gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) causes very high gastrin and multiple ulcers. It is a tumor, and this patient's biopsy shows infection.

questions.stem: Endoscopy also shows a second ulcer on the posterior wall of the gastric body. If this ulcer perforated, into which of the following spaces would gastric contents first leak?
options: Right subphrenic space
Left paracolic gutter
Omental bursa (lesser sac)
Hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch)
approach: The lesser sac (omental bursa) lies directly behind the stomach and lesser omentum, in front of the pancreas.
A perforation through the posterior wall of the stomach therefore opens into the lesser sac first.
Fluid can then pass through the omental (epiploic) foramen into the greater sac.
questions.why: The peritoneal cavity has a large greater sac and a smaller lesser sac behind the stomach. The lesser sac is bounded in front by the stomach and lesser omentum and behind by the pancreas and posterior abdominal wall. It opens into the greater sac only through the omental (epiploic) foramen, which lies behind the free edge of the lesser omentum, the hepatoduodenal ligament. That ligament carries the portal vein, proper hepatic artery, and common bile duct. A posterior gastric perforation therefore fills the lesser sac first and may stay walled off there.
whyNot: The right subphrenic space lies between the liver and diaphragm in the greater sac. Contents from an anterior perforation can reach it.
The left paracolic gutter lies beside the descending colon in the greater sac. Fluid reaches it only after it spreads.
Correct.
The hepatorenal recess is part of the greater sac. Lesser sac fluid can reach it only by passing through the omental foramen.
